body:
Both artifacts ended honestly at the same place: nothing in the material confirms either reading. The account concedes this in its p1, the rival in its r5. The criticism slot arrived empty this cycle, so the account has been challenged only by its own o1 and obliquely by the rival — its central remedy has not had an independent critical pass, and I will not pretend otherwise. What I can mostly contribute is instrument repair: both proposed tests, as stated, can misreport, and the two remedies are less incompatible than the rival suggested.

Start with the compatibility point, because it changes the plan. The rival's r3 says that writing done-ness criteria enacts one side of the contested household question. That is true of unilateral drafting and largely false of shared drafting. If all three flatmates author the note — anyone drafts, everyone edits, nobody merely ratifies — the note becomes an instrument under both readings rather than a remedy under one. How a flatmate edits 'what counts as done' and 'what happens when someone can't' discloses their sense of obligation more safely than a conversation about what the flat 'is.' Someone who strikes the fallback clause and writes 'whoever's around handles it' is telling you something; someone who tightens a deadline is telling you something else; a refusal to touch the draft at all is itself the rival's form-pullback datum. The categories are not neutral, but they are plastic: a unit-reading ('bins rotate') and a privacy-reading ('each handles their own mess') can both be written inside them without anyone declaring a philosophy. So I keep the account's note, accept the rival's enactment warning, and answer it with authorship rather than by abandoning the instrument.

Now the repairs. The account's test — recurrence falls once items are specified — is confounded: recurrence also falls if the avoiding flatmate stops arguing because they have stopped caring. Exit can masquerade as vindication. The gate: success requires recurrence down AND the previously-avoiding flatmate still engaged — doing the item, responding to it, editing the note.

The rival's test — content-engagement versus pullback from the very idea — is confounded by medium. Pullback from a written note may be resistance to writing-as-form, not to being bound. The fix is cheap: re-offer identical content in a lighter medium, a restated verbal agreement or a message thread, and treat persistence across media as the real datum.

My main objection to the rival: withdrawal does not select its reading. r4 maps the avoidance onto the unit-versus-privacy axis, but an exhausted mutual-obligation holder withdraws too — someone who feels they carry the shared side, has stopped raising it, and avoids conversations because each one reopens a grievance ledger. That person is not rejecting obligation; they are burned out on enforcing it. The distinguishing signature is how engagement resumes: the privacy reader disengages from the frame itself; the burned-out enforcer engages with content, but with receipts. This is why the one-to-one ask should carry an explicit past-waiver — 'I'm not here to tally who did what' — since small asks fail most often when heard as openers to an accounting. The waiver serves both candidate populations.

There is also a leaf neither test can see, which the account registered in o1 and both plans then dropped: the trouble may not be about chores at all. Its signature would be engagement that stays warm while nothing chore-specific lands — the friend talks, deflects to other things, and no arrangement changes anything. Keep o1 as a live branch, not a concession.

Sequencing: open with the account's vehicle, not the rival's. r6 — asking each flatmate directly what they take the flat to be — is the wrong first move by the rival's own logic: it reproduces the high-stakes meta-conversation the account correctly warned becomes grievance, and it pre-commits to the rival's framing. Keep that question as a listening target, not an interview question; if the axis is live in this flat it will surface inside a conversation about the bins. The merged opening: one-to-one, one or two recurring items, explicit past-waiver, an invitation to co-author rather than ratify, watching content-versus-frame with one medium retry before any conclusion. Keep the rival's r10 — separate conversations stay separate — but give it an expiry. Once each one-to-one has produced one working item, the three-way conversation must happen; a reader indefinitely carrying positions between two people is its own failure mode.

On zones (r8), take the idea and scope it. Zones relocate specification rather than removing it: the absence-fallback — what happens when the zone's owner is away for a week — survives intact, which is the account's third column still standing. Audit-free ownership is viable only where one person's standard cannot impose on the others: your room, your shelf. Shared infrastructure — kitchen, bathroom — imposes by nature (smell, availability, hygiene), so a floor standard survives even a truce. And there is a price the rival did not name: a zones settlement does not settle the latent contest, it awards it structurally to the privacy reading — privacy claims are divisible by zone, mutual-obligation claims are not. That may still be the right trade; it should be made knowingly.

Both artifacts converge on one endpoint — after repeated, genuinely low-pressure failures, name the question of whether the living arrangement fits — and that convergence is usable as a shared floor whichever reading is true, provided the naming carries no deadline; with one it becomes an ultimatum and undoes everything before it. Two untapped things besides: the third flatmate, whom both artifacts treat as furniture, is both untapped data and a party whose own standards are part of the problem; and the reader's own memory of what each agreement meant is one interpretation among three, so co-authorship is also protection against the reader's certainty.

The ledger. Use: the account's concrete items and fallback column (c2, engagement-gated), its one-to-one opener (c3, past-waiver added), the rival's form-versus-content observation (r7, medium-gated), its zones idea (r8, scoped), its separation rule (r10, expiring), its escalation endpoint (r11, de-pressured), and the account's o1 branch. Revise: u1's success test, r7's test, r6's role, r8's scope, r10's duration. Leave open: which reading holds; the friend's actual reason; pacing — both remedies are pacing-sensitive and neither artifact fixed a window, dense attempts reading as pressure and sparse ones as neglect; whether the arrangement is viable. Reject: nothing outright — but I reject the strong form of r3, that specification is irredeemably one side's enactment, and r6 as a first move.

The standing caution: this cycle repaired instruments; it produced no data. What would move the question is four observations over a week or two — recurrence per item alongside engagement status, which medium was accepted, edit patterns on a co-authored draft, and whether the past-waiver changed anything. Until those exist, the improved decision tree remains a tree about a household none of us can see, and the account's central remedy remains criticized by no one but itself.
